newsitem.title: UK: TABLE TENNIS-CHINA CHASE ANOTHER CLEAN SWEEP.
newsitem.headline: TABLE TENNIS-CHINA CHASE ANOTHER CLEAN SWEEP.

text.p: China, having retained both team titles, go into action in the individual events at the world table tennis championships on Friday aiming to repeat their 1995 unique clean sweep of seven golds.
Players from 115 other countries competing at the G-Mex Centre are intent on preventing another Chinese takeaway but only a handful of them have any chance of derailing the champions.
Chinese team manager Li Furong is anxious to deflect some of the pressure away from his players because of the high expectations.
"It will be very hard to win all seven again," he said. "There are many good players from Europe and Asia with very good techniques.
"We were at home in Tianjin in 1995, it will be much harder this time. We are everybody's target."
China's strength in the men's singles is formidable with defending champion Kong Linghui, Olympic gold medallist Liu Guoliang and World number six Wang Tao spearheading the title assault.

But the 21-year-old Kong appeared vulnerable in the team event, losing to second-seeded 1989 world champion Jan-Ove Waldner of Sweden in the quarter-finals and South Korea's 1988 Olympic gold medallist Yoo Nam-kyu in the semifinals.
Liu went into the team final against France with an unbeaten record but that was spoiled by Patrick Chilla.
In fact, the only Chinese team member to emerge with a 100 percent record was the 29-year-old left-hander Wang, veteran of four world championships.

Waldner, seeded to meet Kong in the final, also had a rocky ride in the team event where the Swedes lost to Belgium in the group stages before succumbing to China in the quarters. Waldner was beaten by Belgium's Philippe Saive and the Belarus world number four Vladimir Samsonov in the group matches and by Toshio Tasaki of Japan in the battle for fifth to eighth places.

Samsonov, who is seeded joint third with Liu, lost to Philippe Saive, although he beat Saive's brother Jean-Michel, the 1993 world champion. Jean-Michele Saive is seeded joint fifth alongside Wang, China's Ding Song and South Korean Kim Taek-soo.
Kim, leading player on the 1996 world all-stars circuit, suffered four defeats in the team matches, including losses to Liu and Wang.
It is difficult to look beyond China in the women's event where defending champion Deng Yaping is hoping to make it two wins in the last three championships, having first held the title in 1991.

The hard-hitting 24-year-old holds the world cup in addition to winning both the singles and doubles titles at the world championships and Atlanta Olympics and her appetite for success is as strong as ever.

The top eight women's seeds are all Chinese although several of them are flying different colours. Second seeded Chen Jing, now playing for Taipei, won the Olympic gold medal in 1988 and the silver at Atlanta eight years later, in addition to being the losing finalist at the 1993 world championships.

Ranked among the 5-8 seeds are Hong Kong's Chai Po Wa, who left mainland China 10 years ago, and Japan's Asian champion Chire Koyama, who was a member of China's 1985 world championship winning team and won the individual title two years later.
